query: For magnetic high-entropy alloys, what single intervention could increase the coercive field? State one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the mechanism expected to alter coercivity, the predicted outcome relative to a matched baseline, the conditions under which the effect should hold, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Cold rolling of equiatomic FeCoNiMnCr high-entropy alloy to 20% thickness reduction at room temperature increases its coercive field by raising dislocation density and thus enhancing domain‐wall pinning.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic FeCoNiMnCr HEA, homogenized and annealed at 1000 °C for 1 h and furnace-cooled (low initial dislocation density).
generation.intervention: Cold rolling to 20% thickness reduction at room temperature.
generation.conditions: Measurements at 25 °C, magnetic hysteresis loops recorded in a vibrating sample magnetometer (1 Hz field sweep) after 24 h stress relaxation.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased dislocation density providing additional domain-wall pinning sites.
generation.mechanism: Dislocations act as obstacles to domain-wall motion, requiring a higher applied magnetic field to overcome pinning and reverse magnetization.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coercive field Hc of the cold-rolled sample will be at least 20% higher than that of the annealed baseline under identical measurement conditions.
generation.baseline: Annealed (1000 °C, 1 h) FeCoNiMnCr HEA with no plastic deformation.
generation.boundary: Applies for thickness reductions up to 25%; beyond this, texture development or dynamic recovery may alter the effect.
generation.uncertainty: Moderate, since competing factors (texture, residual stress relaxation) could modulate coercivity.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of FeCoNiMnCr HEA specimens: one set annealed only, one set annealed then cold-rolled to 20% thickness reduction. After 24 h relaxation, use VSM to measure hysteresis loops at 25 °C. Use TEM to quantify dislocation density and microhardness testing to confirm work hardening.
measurements: Coercive field (Hc) from VSM hysteresis loop
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cold-rolled specimens exhibit less than 5% increase in Hc relative to baseline despite at least a twofold increase in dislocation density, then the hypothesis is falsified.
